Short version: a search request, a recommendation call, or an indexing operation counts as an API call—but the way you manage them depends on whether you're worried about your bill or your site's stability.

### How it Works
In the Algolia ecosystem, API calls generally fall into two buckets: **Search/Discovery** (which drive the shopper experience) and **Indexing/Operations** (which manage your data).

- **Search and Recommend:** Every time a user types a character or a "Related Products" widget loads, it triggers a request. These are generally high-volume and are the primary drivers of your usage.
- **Indexing and Operations:** Adding records, updating synonyms, or changing index settings are considered indexing operations. These are computationally heavier and have their own specific [rate limits](https://support.algolia.com/hc/en-us/articles/41253289629713-Rate-Limits) to ensure system stability.

### Practical Tradeoffs for Ecommerce Teams
The goal is to stop bots from eating your budget without accidentally blocking a high-value customer during a flash sale.

**1. The "Bot vs. Buyer" Balance**
If you use a frontend implementation, you can create a [rate-limited API key](https://support.algolia.com/hc/en-us/articles/15434270755985-Why-is-it-important-to-create-a-rate-limited-API-Key) specifically for your search UI. By setting a limit on queries per hour per IP address, you make it expensive for scrapers to crawl your site while keeping the experience seamless for humans.
*   **Pro tip:** Start with a high limit and gradually tighten it based on your analytics.

**2. Backend Safety**
If your search is routed through your own server (backend implementation), Algolia only sees one IP address—yours. Applying a standard API key restriction here is a mistake because you'll accidentally rate-limit *all* your users at once. In this case, you should handle rate limiting at the server level using a WAF (like Cloudflare) or custom middleware.
